Even worse, the fix brings no new money in, but might break an ancient script at a big customer that relies on the broken error message.

As for "AI will figure things out", that makes as much sense (performance/resource-wise) as running Unix on a PDP-11 emulator written in JavaScript in your browser, but that never stopped anyone, more so as the vendor would get the hardware PO, but the AI tokens would be paid by customers 🤢
comments.name: Ivan Pepelnjak

comments.html:
The thing I am always told is: you will break the test scripts of our test engineers. You will break the test scripts of the platform testers. You will break the scripts of our customers.

So what? If I change something, fix your scripts. No big deal. I always say: if you can't change anything, there will be zero improvement.

The problem is: most managers say they understand that. But they rather see no change at all. They rather have me sitting on my arse, and not do anything. Than do something that might break a test script somewhere. Because doing anything like that will get you noticed. And getting noticed is what you don't want in a big company. Everyone wants to be invisible, sit still, and collect their paychecks. Sitting in meetings is way more safe than actually improving your software.

I committed a 25K line diff 3 weeks ago. It was a cleanup of some technical debt we accrued over the last 25 years. Test managers almost got a heart attack. "It's low risk, trust me. We just need to run existing regressions, and we'll be fine". Nope, stuff needed to be postponed 4 months, so they could make a test plan. Like any tester would actually find any bug in that cleanup.

I also made the mistake of cleaning up/changing some output formatting of some existing show commands. I like to do that. Some of our show commands look like they were done by imbeciles or toddlers. Cleaning things up, making it more readable, more consistent. I know I should not do that. The drama changing even the littlest things is unbelievable. "You added a space, and now our shitty parser broke! Revert your change!".

I could fill this entire blog when horror stories, if Ivan let me. :)

I remember the days when one of our developers was working all day on the new FIB-switching code (that was later renamed to CEF). Every night he uploaded a new IOS image to an ftp server. And all operators of the largest ISPs would upload that new untested image to a few of their core routers and peering routers. Those were the days. I miss those.

(Today I got asked about a bug in software that was released 6 years ago. STFU and just upgrade).
